Pattern of Weight Loss Over Time With Dietary Intervention #16

  • With dietary intervention in overweight and obese adults,
  • average weight loss is maximal at 6 months, with smaller losses maintained for up to 2 years,
  • Weight loss achieved by reducing daily energy intake ranges from 4 kg to 12 kg at 6-month follow-up
  • Thereafter, slow weight regain is observed, with total weight loss at:
  • 1 year of 4 - 10 kg
  • 2 years of 3 - 4 kg
  • 2013 AHA/ACC/TOS Guideline for the Management of Overweight and Obesity in Adults. A Report of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Task Force on Practice Guidelines and The Obesity Society

Slide 17 #17

  • It is estimated that only about 20% of individuals who experience significant weight loss are able to maintain their lost weight.
  • inability of the individual to permanently adopt long-term lifestyle habits that promote a reduced body weight in the face of an obesogenic environment.
  • weight loss  regulatory physiological responses to re-establish positive energy balance  weight regain
  • Wing, R.R. Long-term weight loss maintenance. Am. J. Clin. Nutr. 2005, 82, 222S
  • Keesey, R.E. Body energy homeostasis. Appetite 2008, 51, 442

Barriers in maintaining weight loss  counter-regulation mechanisms #18

  • - Adaptation of energy intake
  • - Adaptation of thermogenesis -  energy consumption
  • Controlled by redundant metabolic, neuroendocrine and autonomic systems

Slide 19 #19

  • The difficulties experienced by individuals who reduce their bodyweight and aim to maintain said reduction reflect the potent counter-regulatory mechanisms.
  • Those include adaptations in EI and adaptive thermogenesis, which are both controlled by redundant metabolic, neuroendocrine, and autonomic systems
  • Mona C. Löffler et al. Mol Metab. 2021 Apr 18;51:101237

Melby C.L., et al #20

  • Nutrients 2017, 9, 468
  • In diet conditions, the magnitude of the initial energy deficit is reduced over time, and energy consumption is reduced as a result of thermogenetic adaptation

Is important to explain to patients #21

  • so that they understand that the
  • lifestyle changes they make need to be sustainable to successfully lose weight and keep it off.
  • JANET FRANKLIN et al. MedicineToday 2020; 21(6): 24-32

Slide 22 #22

  • likelihood of weight regain in weight suppressed obese and formerly obese individuals may be increased by a confluence of biological mechanisms:
  • increased metabolic efficiency,
  • changes in neuroendocrine signaling (e.g., decreased satiety signaling),
  • changes in neural responsivity to both food cues (e.g., increased reward-related or decreased inhibitory anticipatory responsivity) and food intake (e.g., decreased consummatory reward through habituation to the rewarding aspects of palatable food).
  • These biological pressures that may undermine weight loss efforts and promote weight regain are almost immediately enacted in obese individuals attempting even modest and healthy weight reduction.

Slide 23 #23

  • So based on what we now know, what are the lessons learned that can help those people struggling to maintain a healthy weight in our modern “obesogenic environment” conducive to eating more, moving less, and gaining weight at every turn?
  • Yes, weight loss, and even dramatic weight loss, is possible. But it is possible only with major expenditure of time, money, and effort. And the kind of weight loss occurring in “Biggest Loser” contestants is almost impossible to maintain long term when the individuals return to their former environments, away from the 24/7 support system of fitness, nutrition, psychological, and medical staff on the TV series and into an environment where there are competing obligations to family, friends, and jobs. The environment that produced the weight loss included high levels of physical activity, extreme attention to portion control, and strong coaching and support. But this heavy‐duty regimen is not sustainable. Our environment must accommodate a working life and a social life—something “Biggest Loser” participants experienced on their return to the real world.
  • Of the average 58.3 kg lost in 30 weeks of “The Biggest Loser,” 70% was regained over the next 6 years, but the final weight was still 12% lower than before the competition. This is not failure; it is success! Modest weight loss can produce major health benefits , even in individuals with extreme obesity. We are beginning to understand why 5%, 10%, or 15% weight loss has these health benefits.
  • From many studies in which RMR was measured before and after weight loss, it is clear that the metabolic adaptation to lower levels is proportional to the amount of weight loss (spring‐loading model). So this reduction will be much less with more moderate weight loss.
  • In the spring-loading model, the relative strength of adaptive thermogenesis is proportional to the decline in energy stores

Slide 24 #24

  • There is a recognition that obesity management should be about improved health and well-being, and not just weight loss.
  • Shifts the focus of obesity management toward improving patient-centred health outcomes, rather than weight loss alone.
  • Obesity care should be based on evidence-based principles of chronic disease management, must validate patients’ lived experiences, move beyond simplistic approaches of “eat less, move more,” and address the root drivers of obesity.
  • Wharton S. CMAJ 2020 August 4;192:E875-91

Dietary Therapy #28

  • Low-calorie diets (LCD) are recommended for weight loss in overweight and obese persons.

Energy deficit of: #29

  • ≥ 500 – 750 – 1000 kcal/day
  • dietary intake : 1,200 - 1,500 kcal/day for women
  • 1,500 - 1,800 kcal/day for men.
  • Very low-calorie diets - < 800 kcal/day) - in limited circumstances and under medical supervision
  • One of the evidence-based diets that restricts certain food types (as high-carbohydrate foods, low-fiber foods, or high-fat foods)
  • Meal replacements strategies
  • Intermittent fasting
  • Individualized based on the patient’s preferences and health status

  • Hypocaloric diet

Successful weight maintenance programs #34

  • Melby C.L., et al. Nutrients 2017, 9, 468
  • Studies of participants enrolled in the National Weight Control Registry (NWCR) - successfully maintained at least a 13.6 kg weight loss for a minimum of one year, with an average of 33 kg loss maintained for 5 years
  • Predictors of successful weight loss maintenance:
  • frequent weight monitoring,
  • high levels of physical activity,
  • reduced time spent in sedentary activities
  • high levels of dietary restraint,
  • lower calorie and fat intake.

Physical exercise #35

Obesity – Clinical management Physical activity #38

  • Increased physical activity:
  • increased aerobic physical activity (such as brisk walking) for >150 minutes/week (equal to >30 minutes/day, most days of the week).
  • Higher levels of physical activity - 200 - 300 minutes/week, are recommended to maintain lost weight or minimize weight regain long-term (>1 year).
  • Jensen MD, et al. 2013 AHA/ACC/TOS Obesity Guideline

Slide 42 #42

  • Pharmacological treatment should only be considered as part of a comprehensive strategy of disease management.
  • Drug therapy is recommended for patients with a BMI ≥ 30 kg/m 2 or a BMI ≥ 27 kg/m 2 with an obesity-related co-morbidity (HT, T2DM).
  • The efficacy of pharmacotherapy should be evaluated after the first 3 months of therapy (responders).
  • Treatment should be discontinued in non-responders, or – if possible – an alternative therapy should be used.

Bariatric surgery – Indications #46

  • Surgical procedures are the most effective in the medium and long term for inducing weight loss in severely obese patients.
  • The general indications of metabolic surgery are:
  • BMI ≥ 40 kg/m²
  • BMI ≥ 35-40 kg/m² in the presence of comorbidities likely to be improved following surgery
  • BMI ≥ 30-35 kg/m² and uncontrolled type 2 diabetes and/or hypertension with optimal medical therapy.
